listenings.text: Hello, and welcome back to Speak Up, the show for people who live in a second language. Today's topic is a feeling that every one of you knows: being nervous. When I moved to Canada, I used to stay quiet in work meetings. I was afraid of making a mistake. Then a colleague told me something that I have never forgotten. She said that people do not remember your mistakes. They remember your ideas. So this week, here is your challenge. Say one thing in a meeting, or in a shop, that you usually keep inside. It is going to feel strange. Do it anyway.

Hi, Ana Paula! It's Juliana. Guess what? I passed! I got the results this morning, and I have been smiling all day. Do you remember last year, when I almost gave up? I told you that my English wasn't good enough. You said that I just needed time, and you were right. I studied every night after work, and I practiced with my patients. Tonight, my husband and I are going to celebrate at that little Italian restaurant on St. George Street. You have to come! And next year, it's your turn. I know you're going to make it.

extra_audio.text: When I arrived in Florida, I was very nervous. At first, I used to answer everything with yes or no. Then my neighbor told me that my English was good. Since then, I have taken a small risk every week. Next month, I am going to celebrate my first year here.

defs: to get better, little by little
feeling happy because you, or someone you love, did something well
to continue, even when it is difficult
to do something when you are not sure it will go well
a little afraid and worried before something important

the situations where you feel safe and relaxed

paras: When I moved to Jacksonville in 2019, I could read English very well, but I could not speak it. At parties, I used to hide in the kitchen and wash the dishes. I was too nervous to talk to anyone.

Everything changed when my old neighbor, Mr. Collins, knocked on my door. He asked if I could help him with his computer. I made a lot of mistakes that afternoon, but he told me that my English was much better than his computer skills. We both laughed, and I felt proud for the first time.

Since that day, I have taken a risk every week. I have ordered food on the phone, I have complained about a bill, and I have given a short talk at my church. Some weeks I made progress. Other weeks I wanted to give up. But I kept going.

Next month, I am going to celebrate six years in Florida. My advice for people who are learning a language is simple: leave your comfort zone, record your voice, and listen to the recording a year later. You will hear a different person.
